chunks.text: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. Catherine Li ∗ Jingchu Gai ∗ Andrej Risteski Jacob Mitchell Springer † Aditi Raghunathan † Carnegie Mellon University {catheri4, jgai}@andrew.cmu.edu

The Muon optimizer has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s status as the standard optimizer for minimizing pretraining loss ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive.

In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. We show that when tuning pretraining hyperparameters for the lowest pretraining loss, Muon consistently achieves lower loss than AdamW. However, with sufficient pretraining data, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, reversing the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . In Section 4 , we investigate why the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap reverses as the pretraining data budget grows. Fine-tuning changes the output distribution, so we generalize fine-tuning updates with perturbations to the output distribution and study which optimizer produces base models that are more robust to such perturbations. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) , a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits ( Section 4.1 ): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger.

Figure 1: Beyond a sufficiently large data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon. We pretrain OLMo-60M models with Muon and AdamW and fine-tune on StackMathQA. For each pretraining optimizer, we take the pretrained model with the lowest pretraining loss, sweep across all fine-tuning configurations, and plot the resulting learning–forgetting frontier, from 2.4 2.4 B to 38.4 38.4 B pretraining tokens. At 2.4 2.4 B tokens, Muon’s frontier dominates AdamW’s; at larger budgets the trend reverses and AdamW surpasses Muon. This reversal happens despite Muon achieving lower pretraining loss across all data budgets. To understand where this trend comes from, we study a linear associative memory trained with gradient descent (GD) and Muon ( Section 4.2 ). Analyzing a single update from zero initialization, we prove that the ratio of GD’s MSR to Muon’s increases with the data budget ( Section 4.2 ). Simulations of many training steps in the linear associative memory setting confirm the same trend: Muon has the larger MSR at small data budgets, while GD has the larger MSR at large data budgets ( Section 4.2 ). Measuring the MSR of our pretrained language models, we find that Muon has the larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has the larger MSR at large data budgets, mirroring the reversal of the fine-tuning gap ( Section 4.3 ).

Our goal is to compare AdamW- and Muon-pretrained models after fine-tuning . Since fine-tuning can induce forgetting of the pretraining distribution, performance on the fine-tuning task alone is not sufficient: one base model may learn more but also forget more. We therefore compare base models by the tradeoff between the two, and define metrics to track how this comparison changes with model size and pretraining data budget. Fine-tuning gap. We compare the two optimizers on this tradeoff with a single metric, fine-tuning gap G FT G_{\mathrm{FT}} , which we define as the signed mean minimum Euclidean distance between the AdamW and Muon frontier. The fine-tuning gap is positive when the AdamW frontier dominates the Muon frontier, and the reverse else wise. Thus G FT > 0 G_{\mathrm{FT}}>0 when AdamW dominates and G FT < 0 G_{\mathrm{FT}}<0 when Muon dominates ( Section C.5 gives the details). Crossover token–parameter ratio (TPR). We quantify pretraining data budget using token–parameter ratio (TPR), the number of pretraining tokens per model parameter. For a fixed model size and fine-tuning dataset, the crossover TPR is the minimum TPR required for the AdamW frontier to overtake the Muon frontier.

Figure 2: Crossover TPR decreases with model size. In the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, where each pretraining optimizer’s lowest-loss pretrained model is swept across all fine-tuning hyperparameters, Muon’s advantage reverses at substantially smaller pretraining data budgets as model size increases. The exact crossover TPR varies depending on the fine-tuning dataset, but the high-level trend is consistent. We now compare how the learning–forgetting tradeoffs of Muon and AdamW scale with pretraining data budget and model size. In Section 3.2 , we show that as the pretraining data budget increases, Muon’s advantage over AdamW shrinks and eventually reverses in favor of AdamW. This reversal happens at progressively smaller data budgets as model size grows.

Pretraining. We pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens, comparing AdamW and Muon under a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule. We sweep hyperparameters broadly and report the complete pretraining methodology in Appendix C . Fine-tuning. For each base model, we evaluate the learning–forgetting tradeoff on four standard datasets: GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , StackMathQA ( Zhang, 2024 ) , Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) , and MusicPile ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , sweeping AdamW learning rates from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 10 − 2 10^{-2} and Muon learning rates from 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 2 2\times 10^{-2} ( Section C.2 ). We fine-tune AdamW-pretrained models with AdamW and Muon-pretrained models with both AdamW and Muon: AdamW fine-tuning consistently outperforms Muon fine-tuning on AdamW-pretrained models, whereas neither optimizer is consistently better on Muon-pretrained models ( Section D.3 ). We then plot the learning–forgetting frontier over the resulting runs. We choose a broad learning-rate range to ensure we capture the complete learning–forgetting tradeoff spectrum: higher learning rates favor learning at the expense of forgetting, while lower rates preserve pretraining knowledge but learn less.

Evaluating the learning–forgetting tradeoff. For each fine-tuned checkpoint, we compute the fine-tuning loss and pretraining loss on held-out fine-tuning and pretraining (DCLM) data, and use these checkpoints to approximate the learning–forgetting tradeoff. Although this approximation is constructed from a finite set of fine-tuning runs, we conduct a comprehensive sweep over four datasets and across a wide range of fine-tuning learning rates to obtain a close estimate. We evaluate the learning–forgetting tradeoff in two settings: lowest-pretraining-loss setting , and the best-frontier setting . 1. Lowest-pretraining-loss setting : Pretraining hyperparameters are typically selected to minimize pretraining loss. Therefore, for each optimizer, we tune the pretraining hyperparameters to minimize pretraining loss for a given pretraining data budget and model size. We then sweep across all fine-tuning configurations for each of the lowest-loss pretrained models, and evaluate the resulting frontier. 2. Best-frontier setting : However, prior studies find that the lowest-loss pretrained model is not always the best model after fine-tuning: models pretrained with other hyperparameters can offer a better learning–forgetting tradeoff ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, for each pretraining optimizer, we additionally sweep across all pretraining and fine-tuning configurations to achieve the best possible learning–forgetting frontier for a given pretraining data budget and model size ( Section C.1.3 ).

We now investigate how the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap scales with pretraining data budget and model size. Figure 3: The Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap widens with increasing pretraining data budget, and Muon’s advantage shrinks with model size. (a) The fine-tuning gap after fine-tuning OLMo-60M models on StackMathQA, in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting (each pretraining optimizer’s lowest-loss pretrained model swept across all fine-tuning configurations). As the pretraining data budget increases, the fine-tuning gap transitions from negative to positive, with AdamW outperforming Muon beyond the crossover TPR. (b) Pretraining loss at 40 TPR. Muon’s advantage over AdamW shrinks as model size grows. (c) Degradation at 40 TPR, when we accept a StackMathQA loss 10 % 10\% above the best in exchange for less forgetting. Muon degrades increasingly more than AdamW as model size grows. Main result: Pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. We compare the fine-tuning gap for AdamW and Muon at different pretraining data budgets in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, using StackMathQA as the fine-tuning dataset ( Figure 3 a). At small pretraining data budgets ( 2.4 2.4 B tokens), Muon Pareto-dominates AdamW ( Figure 1 ) and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger pretraining data budgets, this trend reverses: beyond 2.4 2.4 B tokens, AdamW achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than Muon. The trend also holds in the best-frontier setting ( Figure 12 ), and for additional fine-tuning datasets in Appendix D . We next investigate how the reversal of the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap scales with model size. Specifically, we ask how the amount of pretraining data needed for AdamW to overtake Muon changes as model size grows.

As model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets. We find that the crossover TPR decreases with model size. On StackMathQA, the crossover is 320 320 TPR for 30M models but only 10 10 TPR for 600M models ( Figure 2 ). The specific crossover TPR depends on the fine-tuning dataset, but the broader trend persists; as model size grows, the crossover TPR decreases, and Muon’s advantage reverses with substantially smaller data budgets. We hypothesize that in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, this scaling trend is driven by two factors: Muon’s shrinking pretraining loss advantage and increased degradation relative to AdamW ( Figure 3 b,c). For each optimizer and model size, we compare its base pretraining loss and its degradation ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) − ℒ PT ​ ( θ PT ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) , after fine-tuning on StackMathQA. First, for a fixed TPR, the gap in pretraining loss between Muon and AdamW shrinks as model size increases, reducing Muon’s advantage as a lower-loss base model. Additionally, for a fixed TPR and fine-tuning loss, Muon forgets increasingly more than AdamW as model size grows. Consequently, as model size scales, Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW narrows, while its forgetting relative to AdamW increases, enabling AdamW to overtake Muon at progressively smaller data budgets.

In Section 3 , we show that Muon offers a better learning–forgetting tradeoff at small token budgets, but AdamW overtakes it beyond a crossover budget. This reversal occurs even though Muon achieves lower pretraining loss at every budget we consider. In this section, we develop a theoretical explanation for this reversal. We compare Muon with exact orthogonalization to full-batch gradient descent (GD), a tractable comparison that captures the qualitative budget trend of Muon and AdamW in language models ( Section 4.3 ). To formalize the relationship between GD and Muon, we study a linear associative memory model of fact learning. In this setting, GD and Muon learn the facts to a similar degree, but their checkpoints can differ in their sensitivity to perturbations of the output distribution. Since fine-tuning changes the output distribution, we expect checkpoints that preserve factual accuracy under a wider range of perturbations to be more resistant to forgetting during fine-tuning. Our central goal is therefore to characterize this sensitivity across pretraining budgets and use it to explain why the forgetting gap reverses. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) : the difference between the correct answer’s logit and the average incorrect logit, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits. The MSR captures a checkpoint’s robustness to output perturbations and provides an analytically tractable basis for comparing GD and Muon.

Roadmap. We introduce the linear associative memory setting, define the MSR, and establish its connection to sensitivity ( Section 4.1 ). We then prove that, after one update step, the ratio of Muon’s MSR to GD’s decreases as the data budget grows, indicating that Muon becomes more sensitive to output perturbations relative to GD ( Section 4.2 ). Finally, we show that the MSR tracks the robustness of AdamW and Muon in real language models ( Section 4.3 ).

Margin-to-spread ratio. In a binary classification problem, a prediction is robust if the correct logit is far from the incorrect logit: the larger the margin, the more robust the prediction. In a multiclass classification problem, such as our linear associative memory setting, there are many incorrect logits. The robustness of a correct output to perturbations of the logits thus depends on its separation from all of the incorrect logits. As it turns out, the degree of separation can be usefully summarized by a single statistic, which we call the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) . MSR captures the average separation between the correct logit and all other logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits. A smaller spread, or a larger average separation, would both place the incorrect logits further below the correct logit relative to their spread, which can increase the robustness of the prediction to perturbations. To capture this intuition, we formally define the margin-to-spread ratio as follows:

chunks.section: 4.2 One-step analysis of the margin-to-spread ratio
chunks.text: We have so far introduced our linear associative memory setup and built intuition for how the MSR captures the robustness of a model to perturbations of its logits. Here, we argue that the MSR of GD is greater than that of Muon for sufficiently large data budgets. We precisely track the one-step dynamics of the MSR ratio ℛ := ρ GD / ρ Muon \mathcal{R}:=\rho^{\mathrm{GD}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} between GD and Muon in the linear associative memory. We analyze a single update from zero initialization, using uniform query weights q i = 1 / N q_{i}=1/N . The weights after many optimization steps depend on the whole training trajectory and are hard to characterize precisely, so theoretical studies of how an optimizer shapes the learned weights often analyze its first step ( Ba et al., 2022 ; Dandi et al., 2024 ; Moniri et al., 2024 ) . Kim et al. (2026) take the same approach to compare a single step of Muon, SGD, and Newton’s method in a linear associative memory.

We test whether the budget trend predicted by Section 4.2 also appears in real language models, beyond the assumptions used in our theoretical analysis. Setup. We evaluate the AdamW and Muon models trained in Section 3 , spanning five model sizes, on held-out DCLM text. We compute the MSR at each token position and report the median over correctly predicted positions. At each position, h h and κ \kappa are the mean and standard deviation of the margins between the correct next-token logit and all other vocabulary logits. We use the median to reduce sensitivity to outliers; Section 4.1 instead uses the mean margin divided by the square root of the mean variance. Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3 . Figure 5: In real language models, the margin-to-spread ratio of AdamW gains on Muon’s as the token budget grows. (a) MSR ρ \rho of AdamW and Muon against pretraining TPR for 30M, 60M, and 100M models: Muon has the larger MSR at small budgets and AdamW at large ones. (b) The MSR ratio ρ AdamW / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{AdamW}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} crosses one as the budget grows, at every model size.

The MSR and fine-tuning crossovers do not necessarily appear at exactly the same budget, since the learning–forgetting tradeoff also depends on pretraining loss. Nevertheless, the MSR captures the direction of the observed shift and connects our theoretical analysis to the behavior of trained language models. Remark. We summarize the analysis of this section and relate MSR to other metrics used to predict post-training. • Takeaway. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the ratio ρ GD / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{GD}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} of the two optimizers’ MSRs increases with the data budget ( Section 4.2 ). Simulations of many training steps show that the same trend persists after extended training ( Section 4.2 ). • Extension: Relation of MSR to Other Metrics Predicting Post-Training. Other work predicts forgetting after post-training with different metrics. For example, Springer et al. (2025) show that the loss increase after adding Gaussian noise to the pretrained weights tracks how much a model degrades under fine-tuning. In Appendix B , we show that MSR is connected to this robustness to Gaussian perturbations: in the linear memory, a larger MSR provably guarantees that more competitors stay ranked below the correct answer after the perturbation ( Section B.2.1 ), and in both language models and the linear memory, MSR is strongly correlated with perturbation robustness ( Section B.2.2 ).

Muon. Muon, an optimizer introduced by Jordan et al. (2024) , has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s dominance as the status-quo optimizer. Recent work has sought to explain Muon’s pretraining advantage through analyses of simplified theoretical models, associative memory, convergence behavior, and loss landscape geometry ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Sato et al., 2025 ; Su, 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Another line of work investigates the training dynamics of Muon, finding that it learns data components more uniformly than AdamW ( Vasudeva et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Dragutinović et al., 2026 ) , while also characterizing the implicit biases of Muon ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Dragutinović et al., 2026 ) . Yet fewer works have examined the downstream consequences of Muon. Ruan et al. (2026) compare Muon and AdamW after fine-tuning; they find that for small data regimes, Muon outperforms AdamW, consistent with our findings. We show that this advantage does not generalize across pretraining data scale; after a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, the trend reverses, and AdamW outperforms Muon.

Muon versus AdamW on pretraining loss. Muon has been reported to reach lower pretraining loss than AdamW for the same compute across a wide range of settings ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Essential AI et al., 2025 ; Mehta et al., 2025 ) , and frontier models have since been pretrained with Muon or its variants ( Kimi Team, 2025 ; GLM-4.5 Team et al., 2025 ) . The size of this advantage depends on scale: under controlled tuning, Muon’s speedup over AdamW shrinks as model size and data grow, and Muon is overtaken by other matrix-based optimizers at large data-to-model ratios ( Wen et al., 2026b ; Wen et al., 2026a ) . All of these works measure pretraining loss. Optimizers can also reach qualitatively different solutions rather than faster or slower routes to the same minimum ( Pascanu et al., 2025 ) ; we ask whether these differences matter after fine-tuning.

Catastrophic forgetting. Catastrophic forgetting, the degradation of previously learned knowledge during subsequent training, remains a central challenge in deep learning ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) . Numerous approaches have been proposed to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, including regularization-based methods ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Zenke et al., 2017 ; Aljundi et al., 2018 ) , replay techniques ( Shin et al., 2017 ) , gradient projection methods ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ; Chaudhry et al., 2019 ) , and optimization-based approaches ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Our learning–forgetting tradeoff is an instance of the stability–plasticity dilemma, with fine-tuning performance capturing plasticity and knowledge retention capturing stability ( Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017 ) . We study forgetting as an intrinsic property of the pretrained checkpoint, rather than as a consequence of the fine-tuning algorithm. Specifically, we investigate how optimization choices during pretraining shape downstream forgetting, showing that Muon and AdamW induce different learning–forgetting tradeoffs.

Pretraining and downstream adaptation. Better pretraining loss does not always yield a better model after fine-tuning. Springer et al. (2025) show that extending pretraining can make language models harder to fine-tune, as the pretrained parameters become increasingly sensitive to modifications, which they measure in part with Gaussian perturbations. Watts et al. (2026) show that sharpness-aware pretraining mitigates forgetting during fine-tuning, and Liu et al. (2026) find that fine-tuning with the same optimizer as pretraining forgets less. We study how the choice of pretraining optimizer interacts with the pretraining data budget, and connect the resulting fine-tuning gap to robustness to weight perturbations.

We asked whether the quality of Muon base models persists through fine-tuning, and found that the answer depends on the pretraining budget: beyond a crossover budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, even though Muon reaches lower pretraining loss. We do not necessarily expect this for every fine-tuning distribution, since fine-tuning on data close to the pretraining data is simply continued pretraining. Still, the trend holds broadly on all datasets we study, including math, instruction following, and music. Furthermore, the crossover budget decreases with model size, which suggests that the problem persists as we scale. We explain why AdamW outperforms Muon at large budgets by tracking how robust each model is to small isotropic perturbations of its output distribution, which we characterize with the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR). AdamW becomes increasingly more robust than Muon as the data budget grows, and this robustness is a property of the output distribution that the training loss does not capture. Since the MSR measures robustness to perturbations of the output distribution in general, our theory suggests that this robustness is fundamental to the checkpoint learned by each optimizer, rather than specific to fine-tuning, to the perturbations we study, or to a particular architecture or parameterization. It should therefore apply to any update that changes the output distribution. Although outside the scope of this work, our analysis suggests that pretraining should explicitly optimize for properties beyond the pretraining loss. Optimizer selection requires more than comparing pretraining loss, and we can design objectives that explicitly target adaptability, for which the MSR is a potential candidate.

More broadly, we expect this lesson to extend beyond Muon. Many pretraining choices, such as hyperparameters, data, and architecture, are selected by pretraining loss. Yet, our results show that pretraining loss can be a poor proxy for adaptability, increasingly so as the data budget grows. This suggests that for any of these choices, a lower pretraining loss does not by itself yield a model that can better adapt.

Optimizers update a model’s parameters during training so as to decrease a loss. Given the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, an optimizer determines the direction and the magnitude of each update, and in doing so shapes training stability, convergence speed and the solution that is finally reached. This section recalls the two optimizers compared in the paper.

Adam ( Kingma & Ba, 2015 ) combines momentum with a per-coordinate step size. With g t = ∇ θ ℒ ​ ( θ t ) g_{t}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t}) the gradient at step t t , it maintains exponential moving averages of the first and second moments of the gradient, m t = β 1 ​ m t − 1 + ( 1 − β 1 ) ​ g t , v t = β 2 ​ v t − 1 + ( 1 − β 2 ) ​ g t 2 , \textstyle m_{t}=\beta_{1}m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{1})g_{t},\qquad v_{t}=\beta_{2}v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_{2})g_{t}^{2}, with the square taken coordinatewise, corrects their bias towards the zero initialization, m ^ t = m t 1 − β 1 t , v ^ t = v t 1 − β 2 t , \textstyle\hat{m}_{t}=\frac{m_{t}}{1-\beta_{1}^{t}},\qquad\hat{v}_{t}=\frac{v_{t}}{1-\beta_{2}^{t}}, and updates θ t + 1 = θ t − α ​ m ^ t v ^ t + ϵ , \textstyle\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\alpha\frac{\hat{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_{t}}+\epsilon}, where α \alpha is the learning rate, β 1 , β 2 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in[0,1) are the decay rates of the two averages, ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 guards the division, and the division and the square root are coordinatewise. In effect each coordinate is normalized by the scale of its own recent gradients. Regularizing Adam with an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} penalty λ 2 ​ ∥ θ ∥ 2 \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\theta\rVert^{2} adds λ ​ θ t \lambda\theta_{t} to g t g_{t} , so the penalty is itself divided by v ^ t + ϵ \sqrt{\hat{v}_{t}}+\epsilon and coordinates with large past gradients are regularized less. AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) instead decouples the weight decay from the adaptive step, θ t + 1 = θ t − α ​ m ^ t v ^ t + ϵ − α ​ λ ​ θ t , \textstyle\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\alpha\frac{\hat{m}_{t}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}_{t}}+\epsilon}-\alpha\lambda\theta_{t},

with g t g_{t} now the gradient of the unregularized loss and λ \lambda the weight decay coefficient, so that every coordinate decays at the same rate. AdamW is the standard optimizer for language-model pretraining and the baseline throughout the paper.

Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) treats each weight matrix as a whole rather than coordinate by coordinate. For a matrix-valued parameter θ \theta with gradient G t G_{t} , it accumulates momentum M t = μ ​ M t − 1 + G t M_{t}=\mu M_{t-1}+G_{t} and updates along the orthogonalized momentum, θ t + 1 = θ t − η ​ Orth ​ ( M t ) , \textstyle\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta\,\mathrm{Orth}(M_{t}), (4) where η \eta is the learning rate and, for a matrix X X with singular value decomposition X = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ X=U\Sigma V^{\top} , Orth ⁡ ( X ) = U ​ V ⊤ \mathrm{Orth}(X)=UV^{\top} is its polar factor: the matrix with the singular vectors of X X and all singular values set to one. The update therefore has the same size along every singular direction, and it can be read as the steepest descent direction when the size of a step is measured in the spectral norm ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . An exact singular value decomposition at every step is expensive, so Orth \mathrm{Orth} is approximated by a few steps of a Newton–Schulz iteration, X 0 = M t ∥ M t ∥ F , X k + 1 = a ​ X k + b ⁡ ( X k ​ X k ⊤ ) ​ X k + c ​ ( X k ​ X k ⊤ ) 2 ​ X k , \textstyle X_{0}=\frac{M_{t}}{\lVert M_{t}\rVert_{F}},\qquad X_{k+1}=aX_{k}+b\,(X_{k}X_{k}^{\top})X_{k}+c\,(X_{k}X_{k}^{\top})^{2}X_{k},

whose odd matrix polynomial pushes every singular value of X 0 X_{0} towards one; the reference implementation uses ( a , b , c ) = ( 3.4445 , − 4.7750 , 2.0315 ) (a,b,c)=(3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315) and five steps. Muon is meant for the two-dimensional weight matrices of the hidden layers; embeddings, the output layer and one-dimensional parameters such as normalization gains are updated by AdamW. Large-scale implementations further add decoupled weight decay and rescale the update to the root-mean-square size of AdamW’s ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . In our experiments the hidden matrices are updated by Muon and all other parameters by AdamW, each with its own learning rate and weight decay ( Section 3.1 ).

All pretraining runs use a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule: the learning rate increases linearly from zero to its peak value over the warmup steps, stays at the peak for most of training, and is annealed to zero over the final decay phase.

All fine-tuning runs use a cosine schedule: after a linear warmup of 20 20 steps, the learning rate follows η t = 1 2 ​ η max ​ ( 1 + cos ⁡ ( π ​ t / T ) ) \eta_{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\eta_{\max}\bigl(1+\cos(\pi t/T)\bigr) over the remaining T T steps.

We measure the pretraining data budget of a model with N N parameters trained on D D tokens by its token–parameter ratio, TPR = D / N \mathrm{TPR}=D/N . The compute-optimal budget of Hoffmann et al. (2022) corresponds to TPR = 20 \mathrm{TPR}=20 ; our budgets range from 5 5 to 2,560 2{,}560 TPR.

chunks.section: Appendix B Other Metrics for Analyzing Post-Training
chunks.text: Besides the margin-to-spread ratio, the robustness of a base model to post-training can be probed by perturbing its weights directly. This section reports Gaussian perturbation results in language models and in the linear memory ( Section B.1 ), and then relates them to the MSR ( Section B.2 ).
We first check whether Gaussian perturbations of the weights reproduce the budget trend of the learning–forgetting tradeoff, in language models and in the linear memory.

We test whether the perturbed loss of the pretrained language models shifts from Muon toward AdamW as the token budget grows, as the learning–forgetting tradeoff does. Setup. Springer et al. (2025) show that adding isotropic Gaussian noise to pretrained weights reproduces key empirical trends in forgetting after fine-tuning. Motivated by this connection, we study Gaussian weight perturbations as a simpler setting in which to investigate why the learning–forgetting gap between Muon and AdamW changes with pretraining budget. At the same checkpoints as in Section 3 , we add isotropic Gaussian noise to each weight matrix, scaled to a fraction δ \delta of the matrix’s norm, and measure the loss increase Δ noise ​ ( θ PT , δ ) := ℒ PT ​ ( θ ~ δ ) − ℒ PT ​ ( θ PT ) \Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}};\delta):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\widetilde{\theta}_{\delta})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) , where θ ~ δ \widetilde{\theta}_{\delta} denotes the perturbed weights; a smaller increase indicates greater perturbation robustness. See Section E.2 for full experimental details. Result. Figure 6 plots the gap in loss degradation, Δ noise ​ ( Muon , δ ) − Δ noise ​ ( AdamW , δ ) \Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}(\text{Muon};\delta)-\Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}(\text{AdamW};\delta) . This gap is positive across the token budgets tested and grows with the pretraining budget: AdamW incurs a smaller loss increase throughout the sweep, and its advantage grows with budget.

To connect this gap to the learning–forgetting tradeoff, we also account for pretraining loss: loss after perturbation equals pretraining loss plus Δ noise \Delta_{\mathrm{noise}} . Muon starts with lower pretraining loss, so it can retain lower loss after perturbation at small budgets despite its larger loss increase. As its pretraining-loss advantage shrinks and the degradation gap grows, AdamW achieves lower loss after perturbation beyond a crossover budget. For sufficiently strong perturbations, this crossover occurs at smaller token budgets as model size increases, paralleling the crossover observed after fine-tuning ( Table 2 in Section E.2 ). Figure 6: The perturbation degradation gap grows with pretraining data budget. Under a perturbation of magnitude δ = 0.02 \delta=0.02 , Muon degrades increasingly more than AdamW as the pretraining data budget grows. Points show the mean over three noise draws.

We repeat the perturbation experiment in the linear memory, where the effect of a perturbation can be measured fact by fact. Setup. We train the memory of Section 4.1 with GD and Muon to minimize cross-entropy, varying the data budget γ = N / d \gamma=N/d and the dimension d d , as in Section 4.2 . The trained weights are perturbed to W ′ = W + σ ​ ∥ W ∥ F ​ ξ W^{\prime}=W+\sigma\lVert W\rVert_{F}\xi with ∥ ξ ∥ F = 1 \lVert\xi\rVert_{F}=1 , over 16 16 perturbation directions shared by the two optimizers. Since the memory retrieves facts, we measure degradation by the fraction of initially recovered facts that are lost. At a single perturbation magnitude, fact loss can be close to zero or one, making memories with different noise tolerances difficult to distinguish. We therefore compare the perturbation strengths needed to reach a common intermediate level of degradation: σ 50 \sigma_{50} is the relative perturbation strength at which half of the initially recovered facts are lost. A larger σ 50 \sigma_{50} means that more noise is needed to cause the same fraction of facts to be lost. Data budgets past the memory’s capacity, where the two optimizers recover different sets of facts, are excluded. Full details appear in Sections E.3 and E.1 . Result. The robustness ordering of the two optimizers turns over with the data budget: Muon tolerates stronger perturbations at small γ \gamma , and GD does at large γ \gamma ( Figure 4 b and the bottom row of Figure 20 ). The σ 50 \sigma_{50} ordering flips at γ ≈ 0.5 \gamma\approx 0.5 , 1.3 1.3 and 11 11 at d = 128 d=128 , 256 256 and 512 512 , and at d = 64 d=64 GD is already the more robust at the smallest data budget we ran.

We test whether the MSR predicts how much perturbation a checkpoint can tolerate, first in language models and then in the linear memory. Language models. We measure MSR as in Section 4.3 and degradation by the held-out loss increase of Section B.1.1 . The robustness threshold δ ∗ \delta^{\ast} is the perturbation magnitude at which this increase reaches Δ ​ L \Delta L nats. Across checkpoints, ρ \rho and δ ∗ \delta^{\ast} are strongly correlated for both Δ ​ L = 0.05 \Delta L=0.05 and 0.1 0.1 ( Figure 7 b): the Spearman correlation over the 72 72 checkpoints is + 0.83 +0.83 at both thresholds, and within each optimizer it is + 0.87 +0.87 to + 0.89 +0.89 for AdamW and + 0.92 +0.92 to + 0.93 +0.93 for Muon. Full experimental details appear in Section E.3 . Linear associative memory. With σ 50 \sigma_{50} as in Section B.1.2 , σ 50 \sigma_{50} is strongly correlated with MSR for both optimizers ( Figure 7 a). Within each optimizer, σ 50 \sigma_{50} and ρ \rho move together at every model dimension ( Figure 23 ). Figure 7: The margin-to-spread ratio tracks robustness to weight perturbations. (a) For the linear models trained under GD and Muon, we plot the perturbation σ 50 \sigma_{50} required to lose half of the recovered facts against its MSR, h ¯ / κ ¯ \bar{h}/\bar{\kappa} ( Section 4.1 ). A higher MSR requires more noise to cause the same loss. (b) We measure the MSR of 72 72 pretrained language models (30M–600M) as the median of h / κ h/\kappa over correctly predicted tokens, and plot the perturbation δ ∗ \delta^{\ast} at which held-out loss rises by Δ ​ L \Delta L . The same relationship holds.

All language models are OLMo-style decoder-only transformers ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) with 30M, 60M, 100M, 300M and 600M parameters, trained on DCLM ( Li et al., 2024 ) with the OLMo 2 tokenizer. Budgets span 5 5 – 1,280 1{,}280 TPR at 30M, 5 5 – 2,560 2{,}560 TPR at 60M, 5 5 – 640 640 TPR at 100M, 5 5 – 160 160 TPR at 300M and 5 5 – 40 40 TPR at 600M.

Every model is pretrained with sequence length 4096 4096 , a global batch of 2 20 2^{20} tokens, a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule, weight decay 0.1 0.1 and gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 . AdamW uses ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.98 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.98) . Muon updates the hidden weight matrices; the remaining parameters (embeddings, output layer and norms) are updated by AdamW.

For each model size, budget and optimizer, we sweep the peak learning rate and call the run with the lowest held-out DCLM loss the loss-optimal base model. For Muon we sweep the Muon learning rate and fix the learning rate of the AdamW-updated parameters to the tuned AdamW value of the same cell ( Section C.1.2 ). Table 1 lists the resulting learning rates. In the lowest-pretraining-loss setting , used throughout the main text, each optimizer is represented by its loss-optimal base model alone: we fine-tune it over the full sweep of Section C.2 and compute the learning–forgetting frontier from its fine-tuning runs. Table 1: Tuned peak pretraining learning rates per model size and budget. For Muon, the Muon learning rate; the AdamW-parameter learning rate is fixed to the tuned AdamW value.

chunks.section: C.1.2 Learning rate of Muon’s AdamW-updated parameters
chunks.text: Muon has a second learning rate for the parameters it leaves to AdamW. Rather than tuning it in every cell, we set it to the tuned AdamW learning rate of the same cell. To check this choice, we pretrain 60M Muon models at 20 20 – 160 160 TPR over a grid of Muon learning rates and three to four AdamW learning rates between 0.5 × 0.5\times and 2.8 × 2.8\times the tuned value. Figure 8 shows the best loss over Muon learning rates for each AdamW learning rate. It varies by at most 0.021 0.021 nats, and the tuned value is within 0.016 0.016 nats of the best, well below the 0.03 0.03 – 0.20 0.20 nats by which Muon beats AdamW at these budgets. Figure 8: Muon is insensitive to the learning rate of its AdamW-updated parameters. Best pretraining loss over Muon learning rates for each AdamW learning rate, relative to the tuned AdamW value (dashed), for 60M models.

The loss-optimal base model is not always the best starting point for fine-tuning: models pretrained with a larger learning rate can offer a better learning–forgetting tradeoff ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . We therefore also compare the two optimizers in the best-frontier setting , which sweeps over both pretraining and fine-tuning configurations. For each model size, budget and pretraining optimizer, we fine-tune the loss-optimal base model and the base models pretrained at the next five larger learning rates of the sweep grid { 0.005 , 0.007 , 0.01 , 0.014 , 0.02 , 0.028 , 0.04 , 0.056 , 0.08 , 0.12 , 0.16 } \{0.005,0.007,0.01,0.014,0.02,0.028,0.04,0.056,0.08,0.12,0.16\} , pool all of their fine-tuning runs, and compute a single learning–forgetting frontier from the pooled runs. This frontier is at least as good as the one of the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, since it contains the loss-optimal base model’s runs. Section D.2 repeats the main results in this setting.

Each base model is fine-tuned for 20M tokens on each of Alpaca ( Taori et al., 2023 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , MusicPile ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) and StackMathQA ( Zhang, 2024 ) , with sequence length 1024 1024 , a global batch of 65,536 65{,}536 tokens (about 305 305 steps), a cosine schedule with 20 20 warmup steps, weight decay 0.1 0.1 , ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) and gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 . AdamW-pretrained models are fine-tuned with AdamW, and Muon-pretrained models with both AdamW and Muon ( Section D.3 motivates this choice). We sweep AdamW learning rates from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and Muon learning rates from 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} to 2 × 10 − 2 2\times 10^{-2} with the learning rate of the AdamW-updated parameters set to 0.25 × 0.25\times the Muon learning rate. The sweep ranges from runs that barely move the base model to runs that reach the lowest fine-tuning loss at the cost of more than a nat of forgetting.

A natural question is whether the reversal survives when fine-tuning itself is regularized to limit forgetting. We test two standard methods for mitigating catastrophic forgetting, data replay ( Shin et al., 2017 ) and elastic weight consolidation ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 , EWC;) , on the loss-optimal base models of every size. Both keep the fine-tuning recipe and learning-rate sweep of Section C.2 , and each frontier pools all strengths of the regularizer. Section D.4 reports the results.

We replace a fraction r ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } r\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3\} of the fine-tuning tokens with DCLM data drawn from a shard that is disjoint from both the pretraining data and the held-out evaluation shard.

EWC penalizes movement away from the pretrained weights in the directions that matter for pretraining. It minimizes ℒ FT ​ ( θ ) + λ 2 ​ ∑ k F k ​ ( θ k − θ PT , k ) 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{k}F_{k}\bigl(\theta_{k}-\theta_{\mathrm{PT},k}\bigr)^{2}, (6) where F F is the diagonal empirical Fisher information of the pretraining loss at θ PT \theta_{\mathrm{PT}} , estimated from squared gradients over 100 100 batches of the disjoint DCLM shard used for replay. Following Watts et al. (2026) , F F is not normalized, so we sweep λ ∈ { 10 3 , 4 ⋅ 10 3 , 10 4 , 4 ⋅ 10 4 } \lambda\in\{10^{3},4\cdot 10^{3},10^{4},4\cdot 10^{4}\} .

We perturb each base model by adding independent isotropic Gaussian noise to every parameter tensor W W , scaled so that ∥ Δ ​ W ∥ F = δ ​ ∥ W ∥ F \lVert\Delta W\rVert_{F}=\delta\lVert W\rVert_{F} , and measure the perturbation degradation Δ noise ​ ( θ PT , δ ) \Delta_{\mathrm{noise}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}};\delta) of Section B.1.1 . We average over three noise draws per checkpoint and magnitude, use the loss-optimal checkpoint of each cell, and consider magnitudes from δ = 0.002 \delta=0.002 to 0.56 0.56 .

Forgetting is the loss on a held-out DCLM shard of about 4.19 4.19 M tokens that no model is trained on, and learning is the loss on the validation split of the fine-tuning dataset. Both are mean next-token cross-entropy in nats.

Each fine-tuned checkpoint θ FT \theta_{\mathrm{FT}} of a base model gives a point ( ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) , ℒ FT ​ ( θ FT ) ) \bigl(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}})\bigr) . We compute the learning–forgetting frontier as the lower-left arc of the convex hull of these points, treated as a polyline.

We estimate the fine-tuning gap G FT G_{\mathrm{FT}} of Section 2 from 100 100 points sampled uniformly by arc length along the AdamW frontier, each assigned its Euclidean distance to the nearest point of the Muon frontier, negative when that point lies closer to the origin. The crossover TPR is the smallest budget at which G FT > 0 G_{\mathrm{FT}}>0 . In both settings, the gap and crossover compare the two optimizers’ frontiers as defined above: one base model per optimizer in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting, pooled base models in the best-frontier setting.

For Figure 3 c, the degradation of a base model is the increase in held-out DCLM loss caused by fine-tuning, ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) − ℒ PT ​ ( θ PT ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{PT}}) . We read ℒ PT ​ ( θ FT ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PT}}(\theta_{\mathrm{FT}}) off the base model’s frontier at a target fine-tuning loss of 1.1 × 1.1\times the lowest fine-tuning loss reached by either optimizer at that model size, so that both optimizers are compared at the same amount of learning.

chunks.section: Appendix D Additional Results for Section 3
chunks.text: This section extends the fine-tuning results of Section 3 . Unless noted otherwise, figures show 60M models, and frontiers are restricted to the region of Section C.5 .

Figure 9 shows that the loss-optimal Muon model reaches a lower pretraining loss than its AdamW counterpart at every budget and model size, so the reversal is not inherited from pretraining loss. Figures 11 and 10 extend the frontiers and gaps of the lowest-pretraining-loss setting ( Figures 1 and 3 ) to all four datasets, at the budgets around each crossover. On every dataset Muon is better than or level with AdamW below the crossover and AdamW is better beyond it. Figure 9: Muon reaches lower pretraining loss than AdamW. DCLM held-out loss of the loss-optimal base models across pretraining data budgets and model sizes. Figure 10: Fine-tuning gap on every fine-tuning dataset, loss-optimal base models (60M). Negative values mean the Muon frontier dominates. Figure 11: Learning–forgetting frontiers on every fine-tuning dataset, loss-optimal base models (60M). Each row shows the budgets around that dataset’s crossover TPR.

We repeat the analyses of Section 3 in the best-frontier setting ( Section C.1.3 ), where each pretraining optimizer is swept across all pretraining and fine-tuning configurations. Figures 13 and 12 show the learning–forgetting frontiers and fine-tuning gaps of 60M models on all four fine-tuning datasets, at the budgets around each crossover. On every dataset, the Muon frontier is better below the crossover; at the crossover AdamW has caught up with or overtaken Muon, and beyond it the AdamW frontier dominates. The fine-tuning gap turns positive at the crossover and stays positive, broadly growing with the data budget. Figure 14 shows that, as in the lowest-pretraining-loss setting ( Figure 2 ), the crossover TPR decreases with model size. Figure 12: Fine-tuning gap on every fine-tuning dataset, best-frontier setting (60M). Negative values mean the Muon frontier dominates. Figure 13: Learning–forgetting frontiers on every fine-tuning dataset, best-frontier setting (60M). Each row shows the budgets around that dataset’s crossover TPR. Figure 14: Crossover TPR decreases with model size, in the best-frontier setting. As model size increases, Muon’s advantage reverses with substantially smaller pretraining data budgets.

Our frontiers fine-tune AdamW-pretrained models with AdamW and Muon-pretrained models with both AdamW and Muon. Figure 15 motivates this choice, and shows that Muon’s greater forgetting at large budgets is a property of the pretrained model rather than of the fine-tuning recipe. For each pretraining optimizer and budget, we take the best 60M base model among those fine-tuned with both optimizers, and plot its AdamW- and Muon-fine-tuned frontiers separately. We use GSM8K, the dataset on which AdamW-pretrained models were fine-tuned with both optimizers across the full range of budgets. Two observations follow. First, the fine-tuning optimizer matters for AdamW-pretrained models but not for Muon-pretrained ones: on AdamW-pretrained models, AdamW fine-tuning dominates Muon fine-tuning at every budget, whereas the two frontiers of a Muon-pretrained model lie close together with no consistent winner. Second, the reversal does not depend on how the Muon-pretrained model is fine-tuned: at 1.2 1.2 B tokens both of its frontiers lie below those of the AdamW-pretrained model, and from 19.2 19.2 B tokens onward the AdamW-pretrained, AdamW-fine-tuned frontier dominates both. Figure 15: Muon’s greater forgetting comes from the pretrained model, not the fine-tuning optimizer. Learning–forgetting frontiers of the best 60M base models on GSM8K, split by fine-tuning optimizer (solid: AdamW; dashed: Muon). AdamW fine-tuning is always better for AdamW-pretrained models, while the two fine-tuning optimizers give nearly the same frontier for Muon-pretrained models. At large budgets, the AdamW-pretrained model dominates under either choice.

We repeat the comparison when fine-tuning is regularized with replay or EWC (setup in Section C.3 ), using the loss-optimal 60M base models. Figures 16 and 17 show the frontiers on all four datasets; each row shows the budgets around that dataset’s crossover under the regularizer, a quarter and half of the crossover TPR, the crossover itself, and four times it. The crossover is the first budget at which the fine-tuning gap turns positive ( Section C.5 ). Both regularizers reduce forgetting and can move the crossover to larger budgets (from 80 80 to 320 320 TPR on Alpaca and StackMathQA), but AdamW’s frontier is better at large budgets on every dataset under both ( Figure 18 ), with one exception: under EWC on StackMathQA the gap turns negative again at the largest budget, 2,560 2{,}560 TPR. With replay, Muon’s frontier is better than or level with AdamW’s below the crossover on every dataset. With EWC the picture below the crossover is mixed: Muon is clearly better at small budgets on GSM8K, while on the other datasets the two frontiers are close. Figure 16: Learning–forgetting frontiers with replay of 10 10 – 30 % 30\% DCLM data, loss-optimal 60M base models. Each row shows the budgets around that dataset’s crossover under replay. Figure 17: Learning–forgetting frontiers with EWC , λ ∈ { 10 3 , 4 ⋅ 10 3 , 10 4 , 4 ⋅ 10 4 } \lambda\in\{10^{3},4\cdot 10^{3},10^{4},4\cdot 10^{4}\} , loss-optimal 60M base models. Each row shows the budgets around that dataset’s crossover under EWC. Figure 18: Fine-tuning gap under fine-tuning regularization , with replay (solid) and EWC (dashed), loss-optimal 60M base models. Negative values mean the Muon frontier dominates.

Experimental Result. Figure 5

Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3
